title: Fortinet Enterprise Networking & Security — Daily Examination

questions.question: A maintenance window is planned on one eBGP path. The backup path must become preferred before the peer session closes. What should the receiving peer do?
choices: Match the gshut community and lower local preference on those routes
Increase the hold timer and wait for the neighbor to reset
Apply a route map that removes every route from the peer
Disable BFD and rely on the default BGP keepalive timer
feedback: Correct: the receiver recognizes the well-known graceful-shutdown community and de-preferences the marked path before withdrawal.
Changing hold timers delays failure detection but does not drain traffic onto an alternate path.
Removing every route is an abrupt withdrawal, not a controlled preference transition.
BFD is a separate liveness detector; disabling it alone does not implement graceful route draining.

questions.question: A team wants to drain traffic temporarily but keep the BGP session established. Which graceful-shutdown behavior fits?
choices: Graceful mode closes the session after the configured delay
Graceful-soft mode de-preferences routes and restores preference later
A route refresh immediately removes every route from the peer
Graceful restart preserves stale routes after a control-plane restart
feedback: Graceful mode is intended to close the peer session after the drain interval.
Correct: graceful-soft keeps the session up, temporarily lowers preference, then restores it after the delay.
A route refresh is not the graceful-shutdown state machine and does not perform this timed drain.
Graceful restart addresses restart recovery and stale-route retention, not planned route draining.

questions.question: During a drain, the BGP summary reports `In gshut`. Which additional evidence best confirms traffic can move to the backup?
choices: The peer uptime counter continues increasing
The marked route has gshut community and lower local preference than the alternate
The interface reports carrier up and full duplex
The neighbor's configured keepalive interval matches the remote value
feedback: Peer uptime alone does not show that route preference changed or that a backup exists.
Correct: the community and lower local preference show the intended route de-preference; confirm the alternate is best in the routing table.
Carrier state proves physical link state, not BGP best-path selection.
Matching keepalive values show timer agreement, not route-drain completion.

questions.question: A site has only one usable upstream route. The operator enables graceful shutdown and waits for the delay. What is the likely outcome?
choices: Traffic remains on the old path because gshut pins the route
The route is copied into the local routing table as a backup
The receiver synthesizes an alternate route from the community value
The route is withdrawn after the drain and traffic loses its only path
feedback: The community does not pin traffic to a path; it changes route preference.
A backup route must already exist and be eligible; graceful shutdown does not clone routes.
The gshut community is a signal, not a route-generation instruction.
Correct: without an eligible alternate, closing the session removes the only path and can cause an outage.

questions.question: A password-type object already exists in the ADOM. During import from a PDE-enabled FortiGate, the goal is to retain the live device password. What should the operator enter?
choices: Leave the existing-object password field blank to preserve the current device value
Enter the object name again so FortiManager can decrypt the value
Enter a random value and let the next install reconcile it
Delete the ADOM object before importing the device configuration
feedback: Correct: the documented blank choice preserves the current FortiGate password for an existing object.
Object names do not decrypt private data or recover the secret.
A random value changes the intended credential and can break dependent services.
Deleting the object is unnecessary and can break references or policy packages.

questions.question: A newly discovered password-type object appears in the FortiManager import wizard. Which action completes the documented import handling?
choices: Skip every password prompt because PDE objects are imported automatically
Use the ADOM name as the password for all imported objects
Provide the password for each new password-type object when prompted
Disable private data encryption on the FortiGate before every import
feedback: Skipping the prompt can leave the imported object without the required secret value.
The ADOM name is unrelated to the device's password-type object value.
Correct: the import flow prompts for the secret material for each new password-type object.
Disabling PDE is not required by the documented FortiManager 8.0 import workflow.

questions.question: The import finishes, but a later install preview shows an unexpected object change. Which review is most useful before pushing?
choices: Check the device serial number only and proceed if it matches
Review duplicate-object resolution, object references and the install preview delta
Re-enter every secret in the ADOM without checking object references
Run a firmware upgrade so the import database is rebuilt
feedback: A matching serial number does not explain an unexpected object or secret delta.
Correct: duplicate handling, references and the install preview reveal what will actually be installed.
Blindly re-entering secrets may overwrite correct values and still leave bad references.
A firmware upgrade is unrelated to the object import transaction.

questions.question: An engineer assumes importing a PDE-protected object automatically rotates the password on the managed FortiGate. Which statement is accurate?
choices: Importing the object always forces a password change on the source device
The password is converted into plaintext and stored in the ADOM
The import process disables the device's PDE setting after synchronization
Import handles the object value; device credential changes remain a separate install decision
feedback: The source device password is not automatically rotated just because the object was imported.
The documented workflow does not describe plaintext conversion as the import result.
The import feature does not disable the FortiGate's PDE setting.
Correct: distinguish object import and secret handling from the later device installation/change transaction.

questions.question: A FortiData Risk Record is visible in Log Browse but does not create an Event Monitor alert. What is the best next step?
choices: Create a custom event handler for the Risk Record log type
Reinstall the FortiData device because Log Browse is only a cache
Increase the FortiAnalyzer log disk quota before checking handlers
Disable the Ingested External Alerts handler and restart the SIEM database
feedback: Correct: the predefined handler triggers on FortiData Issue logs; Risk Record and Integration Event need custom handlers.
Log Browse visibility proves raw receipt, not that the device is misregistered.
Disk quota is not the first explanation when the raw record is already visible.
Disabling the default handler removes the existing Issue alert path and does not add Risk Record handling.

questions.question: Which FortiData incident type is handled by the predefined Ingested External Alerts event handler?
choices: Integration Event records from every FortiData connector
Risk Record logs only after manual normalization
Issue logs received from the FortiData device
Every Xlog record after it is inserted into siemdb
feedback: Integration Event logs require their own custom event-handler logic.
Risk Record logs are supported, but are not the default handler's documented trigger.
Correct: the predefined handler is enabled by default and triggers alerts from FortiData Issue logs.
Database insertion does not automatically turn every Xlog type into an alert.

questions.question: FortiData Xlog files are visible in Log Browse, but the records are absent from Logs > All. Which boundary should be investigated?
choices: The Event Monitor notification destination
The SIEM database insertion stage after raw-file receipt
The FortiData device's physical power supply
The browser cache used by the FortiAnalyzer administrator
feedback: Notification delivery occurs after event-handler processing and does not explain missing database records.
Correct: Log Browse proves raw receipt; Logs > All depends on insertion into siemdb.
Power loss is unlikely when new Xlog files are already arriving.
Browser cache does not control server-side insertion into siemdb.

questions.question: An Issue log creates an Event Monitor alert. What does that result prove most directly?
choices: All three FortiData incident types have default alert rules
Every Xlog field was normalized into every report schema
The FortiData device is now authorized to change FortiGate policies
The Issue record reached the configured event-handler path
feedback: Risk Record and Integration Event still need custom handlers.
An alert does not prove every field is available in every report schema.
FortiData alerting does not automatically grant policy-change authority on FortiGate.
Correct: the alert proves that the Issue record reached and matched the event-handler path.

questions.question: FortiGate can reach a managed FortiSwitch, but configuration synchronization fails after trusted hosts were restricted. What should be checked first?
choices: Add the actual FortiLink source subnet to the switch administrator's trusted hosts
Disable FortiLink discovery so the switch uses its management interface
Replace the switch admin account with a local read-only account
Change the switch native VLAN to match the FortiLink subnet
feedback: Correct: FortiGate uses its FortiLink source address for REST API login and configuration pushes.
Disabling discovery does not repair a trusted-host source mismatch.
A read-only account cannot complete the required configuration synchronization.
The trusted-host list is an administrator source restriction, not a native-VLAN mapping.

questions.question: A managed switch uses Layer-3 FortiLink. The administrator enables `set auto` in the admin security policy. What should they expect?
choices: FortiLink addresses are always inferred from the first DHCP lease
The policy creates a new default route for the switch
Auto assignment is ignored for Layer-3 FortiLink; trusted hosts must be entered manually
The switch falls back to standalone administrator authentication
feedback: The documented behavior does not infer trusted hosts from an arbitrary DHCP lease.
Trusted-host assignment does not create a routing entry.
Correct: FortiLink auto-assignment is ignored for Layer-3 FortiLink, so enter the allowed addresses explicitly.
Layer-3 FortiLink does not force the switch into standalone mode.

questions.question: A FortiSwitch is managed through a NAT path. Why can automatic trusted-host assignment block FortiGate management?
choices: The FortiLink interface stops sending REST API requests after NAT is detected
The address pushed automatically may not match the source address seen by the switch
IPv6 trusted hosts are disabled whenever IPv4 NAT is present
The switch converts every FortiLink address into a VLAN interface
feedback: NAT does not automatically stop REST API requests; it changes the source identity seen downstream.
Correct: the auto-populated address may be wrong across NAT, so explicit trusted hosts are safer.
IPv6 trusted-host configuration is not disabled merely because IPv4 NAT exists.
Trusted-host assignment does not convert addresses into VLAN interfaces.

questions.question: `execute switch-controller get-sync-status all` shows the switch online but CONFIG remains unsynchronized. What is the most relevant test?
choices: Check whether the switch has enough PoE budget for the FortiGate
Replace the FortiLink interface with a standalone trunk
Clear the switch MAC table and wait for STP convergence
Verify FortiLink source IP is allowed by the switch admin trusted-host list
feedback: PoE budget does not explain an authenticated configuration-push failure.
Replacing FortiLink changes the design without addressing the management access list.
MAC learning and STP convergence are separate from the REST API login boundary.
Correct: the FortiLink source must pass trusted-host validation before configuration synchronization succeeds.

questions.question: A FortiAP is connected to a switch port using 802.1X. The switch blocks CAPWAP traffic until authentication succeeds. Which component must authenticate first?
choices: The FortiAP wired-uplink supplicant
Every wireless client using the AP's SSID
The FortiGate controller using the AP's radio MAC
The AP's CAPWAP tunnel after it receives an IP address
feedback: Correct: the FortiAP itself acts as the 802.1X supplicant on its wired LAN port.
Wireless-client authentication happens after the AP has joined and advertises the SSID.
The controller is not the supplicant on the access switch port.
CAPWAP cannot traverse a port that is still blocking non-EAP traffic.

questions.question: A FortiAP profile uses EAP-TLS, but the wired switch port remains unauthorized. Which check is most specific to the AP supplicant?
choices: Verify the client SSID's RADIUS VLAN attribute
Change the AP's radio band to 5 GHz only
Inspect CA, client certificate and private-key material with `cw_diag -c wan1x`
Disable CAPWAP encryption on the FortiGate controller
feedback: The wireless SSID VLAN attribute is not the AP's wired-uplink EAP-TLS credential.
Changing the radio band does not fix certificate-based wired authentication.
Correct: the AP supplicant requires valid trust and client credential material; the command exposes the installed certificate state.
CAPWAP encryption is downstream of wired-port authorization and is not the first failure boundary.

questions.question: `cw_diag -c wan1x` reports `Port Status: Authorized`. What has been proven?
choices: The AP has joined the correct FortiGate and is serving clients
The wired 802.1X supplicant has been authorized by the access network
Every wireless client has completed its own 802.1X exchange
The AP's radio channels have passed DARRP optimization
feedback: Authorization on the wired port does not prove controller discovery or join completion.
Correct: the supplicant's wired access-control transaction succeeded.
Wireless clients authenticate separately through the SSID's security configuration.
DARRP is a radio-channel planning process, not wired-port authorization.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes FortiAP uplink 802.1X from client 802.1X on an SSID?
choices: Both authenticate the same wireless station and share one EAP transaction
Uplink 802.1X occurs only after the AP has joined its controller
The switch authenticates the FortiGate controller through the AP radio
Uplink 802.1X authenticates the AP device before normal wired traffic is admitted
feedback: The AP and wireless station are different supplicants in different authentication transactions.
Uplink authentication is required before ordinary AP traffic and controller join can proceed.
The access switch sees the AP's wired supplicant, not the FortiGate controller through radio.
Correct: the AP authenticates as a wired endpoint before its normal traffic is allowed.

questions.question: An IPv6-only workstation reaches the FortiNAC portal and runs the agent, but an IPv6-only switch is absent from Inventory. What explains the difference?
choices: IPv6 is supported for endpoint portal/agent access, while device discovery still needs IPv4
FortiNAC disables IPv6 whenever an endpoint uses an agent
The portal translates every IPv6 address into a discovered switch record
Inventory discovery requires an IPv4 address on the network device
feedback: Correct: FortiNAC supports IPv6 endpoint communication but its network-device management/discovery path still requires IPv4.
Agent use does not disable IPv6 endpoint access.
Portal access does not synthesize managed network-device inventory records.
This is the documented limitation: network devices in Inventory need IPv4 management reachability.

questions.question: Which FortiNAC interface roles are documented for IPv6 portal/agent access and administrative UI access?
choices: eth0 for portal and eth1 for administrative UI
eth1 for inventory discovery and eth0 for switch polling
eth1 for portal/agent traffic and eth0 for administrative UI
Both interfaces are restricted to IPv4 while only host records use IPv6
feedback: The roles are reversed in this option.
Inventory discovery remains an IPv4 management function; it is not the eth1 portal role.
Correct: eth1 supports portal/agent communication and eth0 supports the admin UI over IPv6.
FortiNAC supports IPv6 on both interfaces for the documented endpoint/admin paths.

questions.question: An IPv6 address appears in Host View and Adapter View. What is the safest interpretation?
choices: The switch inventory is now fully manageable over IPv6
The endpoint record contains IPv6 address information; device discovery is a separate capability
Every L3 polling vendor now supports IPv6 device management
The FortiNAC admin UI must have moved to the endpoint's address
feedback: Host address display does not imply switch discovery or management.
Correct: host/adapter visibility proves endpoint address handling, not IPv6-only network-device inventory support.
The guide lists specific L3 polling support and does not claim universal IPv6 management.
The endpoint's address and the admin UI's interface address are separate identities.

questions.question: A campus wants IPv6-only workstations but retains IPv4 management for switches. Which design matches the documented support boundary?
choices: Move the portal to eth0 and disable the IPv4 management network
Use IPv6 for all Inventory polling and rely on the agent for switch discovery
Convert every switch management address into an IPv6 link-local address
Keep endpoint portal/agent paths dual-stack while retaining IPv4 device-management addresses
feedback: The documented portal path is eth1; moving it does not remove the Inventory IPv4 requirement.
The agent does not replace network-device management/discovery.
Link-local addressing does not provide the required managed-device reachability.
Correct: endpoint access may use IPv6 while the separate Inventory device-management plane retains IPv4.

questions.question: A TEAP client authenticates to local RADIUS. Which sequence describes the protocol's two main phases?
choices: TLS establishes an outer protected tunnel, then inner EAP methods authenticate identities
Inner MSCHAPv2 completes first, then TLS encrypts the finished RADIUS packet
The client sends a PAC before the server validates its certificate
The RADIUS server proxies every TEAP exchange to an external server
feedback: Correct: TEAP first establishes the TLS tunnel, then conducts inner authentication and authorization conversation.
The inner method is protected by the outer tunnel, not completed before it.
PAC use is part of fast resumption/provisioning behavior, not a substitute for the initial TLS phase.
FortiNAC-F local RADIUS can process TEAP without proxying the EAP exchange externally.

questions.question: The outer TEAP TLS handshake succeeds, but the user authentication fails inside the tunnel. Where should troubleshooting focus?
choices: The switch's native VLAN and spanning-tree root priority
The AP's CAPWAP controller discovery address
The configured inner EAP method and Winbind/AD dependency
The FortiNAC Manager's N+1 secondary CA promotion state
feedback: A native VLAN issue may affect access after authentication, not inner EAP credential validation.
CAPWAP is unrelated to this wired RADIUS TEAP exchange.
Correct: inner EAP-MSCHAPv2/EAP-TLS and the configured directory/Winbind path are the next transaction stage.
N+1 CA promotion is a separate availability mechanism.

questions.question: A TEAP deployment uses PAC-based fast reauthentication. What does the PAC opaque key protect?
choices: The switch's RADIUS shared secret and VLAN assignment
The PAC contents so they remain confidential and tamper-resistant
The FortiNAC Manager database backup and synchronization queue
The client certificate's public key during the initial TLS handshake
feedback: The RADIUS shared secret and VLAN attributes are not the PAC opaque-key payload.
Correct: the opaque key encrypts and validates the 32-byte PAC used for protected session resumption.
Manager database backup is unrelated to TEAP PAC handling.
The TLS handshake validates certificates independently of the PAC opaque key.

questions.question: The TEAP exchange completes successfully, but the endpoint lands in the isolation VLAN. What is the next boundary to inspect?
choices: Increase the TLS record size until the VLAN changes
Replace the PAC opaque key without checking authentication logs
Disable the secondary inner EAP method for every user
Review the matched Network Access Policy and its VLAN authorization
feedback: TLS record size does not select the authorized VLAN.
PAC changes are not justified when the TEAP exchange already completes.
Disabling secondary authentication may weaken policy and does not correct VLAN mapping.
Correct: successful authentication and network authorization are separate; inspect the matched policy and VLAN decision.

questions.question: A RADSec client opens TLS to FortiAuthenticator but the handshake is rejected before RADIUS processing. Which trust check is decisive?
choices: The client certificate must chain to a configured Local CA or Trusted CA
The RADIUS shared secret must equal the TLS server certificate password
The client must use the same hostname as the FortiAuthenticator appliance
The accounting packet must contain an Access-Accept attribute
feedback: Correct: FortiAuthenticator validates the RADSec client's certificate against configured Local or Trusted CAs.
The RADIUS shared secret is separate from TLS client-certificate validation.
The certificate identity and configured trust matter; identical hostnames are not the rule.
Accounting is processed after the TLS session and decryption, not used to validate the handshake.

questions.question: Which server-side setting and port are central to the documented RADSec listener setup?
choices: Use the EAP server certificate on UDP/1812 only
Enable plain RADIUS on UDP/1645 and disable TLS
Select the RADSec server certificate and use the configured RADSec service port
Configure a wildcard EAP certificate and listen on TCP/443
feedback: EAP server certificates are distinct from the RADSec server certificate.
Plain UDP RADIUS is not the RADSec TLS listener.
Correct: the RADSec server certificate is configured separately; the default RADSec port is 2083.
FortiAuthenticator does not support wildcard certificates for the EAP server, and TCP/443 is not the default RADSec port.

questions.question: FortiAuthenticator 8.0 supports RADIUS accounting over RADSec, but a FortiSwitch integration does not send accounting or CoA over RADSec. What is the correct conclusion?
choices: The FortiAuthenticator feature is disabled whenever a switch is managed
Client interoperability must be checked; server support does not guarantee every client message type
The FortiSwitch should send accounting as a TLS certificate extension
The RADIUS daemon must be replaced with a second RADSec service
feedback: Management state does not globally disable FortiAuthenticator RADSec accounting.
Correct: the server can support accounting while a specific client integration has narrower support.
Accounting is a RADIUS message, not a certificate extension.
The existing RADIUS daemon processes decrypted requests; replacing it is not required.

questions.question: A design proposes 700 simultaneous RADSec clients to one FortiAuthenticator. Which documented capacity fact matters?
choices: The default listener is limited to 50 clients
RADSec uses one TLS connection for every RADIUS attribute
The client count is unlimited when accounting is enabled
The documented maximum is 500 simultaneous RADSec clients
feedback: The documented maximum is not 50.
RADIUS attributes do not each require separate TLS sessions.
Accounting support does not remove the documented client capacity.
Correct: the guide states a maximum of 500 simultaneous RADSec clients.

questions.question: A privileged Java client runs as `java.exe`, but its launch arguments uniquely identify the application. Which matcher is most appropriate?
choices: Command Line matcher with a tested regular expression
Default matcher using the initial executable only
Window Title matcher using the Windows user name
Process ID matcher using the value from yesterday's session
feedback: Correct: command-line matching can distinguish Java applications that share java.exe but use different arguments.
Default executable tracking is the behavior this scenario has outgrown.
A user name is not a window-title signature.
Process IDs change between launches and are not the documented matcher type.

questions.question: An administrator changes a launcher from Default to Window Title matching. Which capture behavior is enforced?
choices: Only the matched window is recorded and child processes are ignored
The secret is converted into an agentless session
Multiprocess Mode and full-screen recording are forced enabled
The launcher stops recording until the user checks out the secret
feedback: The documented safety behavior is broader process-tree and full-screen capture, not window-only capture.
The matcher does not change FortiPAM into agentless mode.
Correct: non-default matchers force multiprocess observation and full-screen recording to preserve the audit trail.
Secret checkout is unrelated to the process matcher setting.

questions.question: A Windows application renames its window during startup, while its command line remains stable. Which matcher is the safer choice?
choices: Window Title with a regex that matches the transient title
Command Line with a regex tied to stable launch arguments
Default matching against the initial process name only
A fixed process ID copied from the launcher configuration
feedback: A changing title makes a title-based regex brittle.
Correct: stable command-line arguments provide a better signature for this application.
Default matching is less useful when the process tree changes or spawns children.
A process ID is runtime-specific and should not be configured as an application identity.

questions.question: A Window Title regex matches both the privileged client and an unrelated support tool. What is the best correction?
choices: Disable full-screen recording so fewer processes are visible
Change the target secret password and relaunch the session
Switch to Default matching without validating the process tree
Anchor and narrow the regex against actual runtime window titles
feedback: Reducing recording scope weakens audit coverage and does not correct the matcher.
A target password does not affect window-title matching.
Returning to Default may restore the original false negative.
Correct: test the regex against real titles and constrain it to the intended application.

questions.question: A Windows Agent is online in CMDB, but no certificate lifecycle events appear. Which deployment step is most often missed?
choices: Associate the certificate-monitoring template with the host and Apply it
Restart the Windows host after every certificate scan
Create a FortiSIEM collector for UDP/514 certificate syslog
Change the Windows host's DNS suffix to the event type name
feedback: Correct: the Supervisor distributes monitoring policies only after template association and Apply.
The documented workflow does not require rebooting for each certificate scan.
Certificate monitoring is delivered by the Windows Agent, not a generic syslog collector.
DNS suffixes do not control the agent's certificate event types.

questions.question: Which event type should an analyst search for when a monitored Windows certificate is approaching expiration?
choices: AO-WUA-Certificate-Removed
AO-WUA-Certificate-Added
AO-WUA-Certificate-Expiring
AO-WUA-Registry-Modified
feedback: Removed indicates a certificate was deleted, not that it is nearing expiry.
Added indicates a new certificate was detected.
Correct: AO-WUA-Certificate-Expiring identifies the certificate approaching its configured expiration window.
Registry modification is a different monitoring event family.

questions.question: A host reports certificate additions and removals but no expiration alerts. What should be reviewed first?
choices: The FortiGate SD-WAN Performance SLA target list
The certificate monitor template's expiry window and the exact AO-WUA event family
The FortiSIEM incident graph layout and node colors
The Windows Agent's TCP segmentation offload setting
feedback: SD-WAN target selection has no role in Windows certificate lifecycle monitoring.
Correct: expiration thresholds are configurable, and the event family distinguishes expiring from added/removed.
Investigation graph layout does not create the underlying certificate event.
TSO is unrelated to certificate monitoring policy.

questions.question: The security team wants alerts 21 days before a Windows certificate expires. Which setting aligns with the documented feature?
choices: A fixed 90-day certificate renewal window
A Windows Event Log subscription for every registry key
A daily PowerShell job that exports the certificate store
A configurable 7-to-30-day certificate expiry window
feedback: Ninety days is outside the documented configurable 7-30 day window.
Registry subscriptions are not the certificate-monitoring control.
A custom script is not required for the documented agent feature.
Correct: 21 days is within the documented configurable expiration range.

questions.question: An administrator defines an agent-based ZTNA destination as a CIDR subnet, but the instance uses an older default FortiClient baseline. What requirement should be checked?
choices: Feature-version eligibility and default FortiClient 7.2.8 or later
The FortiSASE portal's custom domain certificate and DNS CNAME
The FortiGate BGP graceful-shutdown community on the gateway
The FortiNAC Inventory IPv4 address of the remote endpoint
feedback: Correct: the feature requires the Feature version and default FortiClient 7.2.8 or later.
Custom domain/certificate is an agentless ZTNA feature, not the agent-based subnet requirement.
BGP graceful shutdown is unrelated to endpoint destination objects.
FortiNAC Inventory address requirements do not control FortiSASE ZTNA host definitions.

questions.question: A private application is reachable through an agent-based ZTNA destination object, but users can connect to more ports than intended. What should be tightened?
choices: The FortiClient endpoint display name
The FortiSASE instance's NTP server list
The destination object's port list or port range
The FortiNAC endpoint's IPv6 portal address
feedback: The endpoint display name does not define the network service scope.
NTP settings do not determine allowed application ports.
Correct: narrow the destination port list/range to the services that users require.
FortiNAC portal addressing is unrelated to FortiSASE ZTNA destination port enforcement.

questions.question: Which deployment description correctly identifies agent-based rather than agentless ZTNA?
choices: Browser bookmark access through a custom-domain portal only
FortiClient on the endpoint receives destination and gateway policy
A switch port authenticates an AP using EAP-PEAP
A RADIUS server proxies every private application connection
feedback: A browser bookmark portal describes the agentless access pattern.
Correct: agent-based ZTNA relies on FortiClient endpoint configuration and the destination object.
This is wired 802.1X for a FortiAP, not ZTNA.
RADIUS authentication is not the data-plane proxy for every private application connection.

questions.question: The destination subnet and port scope look correct in the console, but one managed endpoint cannot access the application. What is the next configuration check?
choices: Rebuild the FortiGate BGP neighbor table
Disable the endpoint firewall and retest without policy
Change the FortiSASE tenant's billing region
Confirm the endpoint profile assigns the correct ZTNA gateway and destination
feedback: BGP state does not establish the endpoint's ZTNA application assignment.
Disabling endpoint protection is not a supported first diagnostic step.
Billing region does not determine destination assignment to a client profile.
Correct: the endpoint must receive the destination through the assigned profile and gateway.

questions.question: The FortiGuard SLA database cannot be downloaded or updated on a new FortiGate. Which prerequisite should be verified?
choices: A valid SD-WAN Underlay and Application Monitoring license
A FortiNAC-F TEAP license and local RADIUS certificate
A FortiPAM launcher process matcher profile
A FortiSwitch admin trusted-host security policy
feedback: Correct: FortiGate requires the SD-WAN Underlay and Application Monitoring license for the SLA database.
TEAP licensing and RADIUS certificates are unrelated to FortiGuard SLA targets.
FortiPAM launcher matching does not control SD-WAN licensing.
Switch administrator trusted hosts do not affect the FortiGate SLA database entitlement.

questions.question: The Performance SLA table shows a green up arrow beside a probe server, but the service rule still avoids that member. What does the arrow prove?
choices: The member meets every latency, jitter and loss threshold
The application is reachable through every SD-WAN zone
The probe server is responding, not that the SLA thresholds are met
The service rule has selected that member for all sessions
feedback: A responding server does not imply the measured quality meets the configured thresholds.
The arrow does not prove reachability through every zone or application path.
Correct: server response and SLA quality are separate states.
The service rule may still choose another member based on quality and strategy.

questions.question: An engineer selects a FortiGuard SLA target for a SaaS service. Which additional configuration makes the measurement meaningful?
choices: Enable the database and assume every member is automatically tested
Choose the protocol, participating SD-WAN members and quality thresholds
Create a static route to the FortiGuard database server only
Set the SLA name to the SaaS provider's registered trademark
feedback: Enabling the database supplies targets, not the full health-check definition.
Correct: protocol, participants and thresholds determine what is measured and how steering uses it.
A static route to the database server does not define the application probe path.
The SLA name is descriptive metadata, not a steering input.

questions.question: A FortiGuard target is unreachable from one member, while a second configured server responds. What is the most useful interpretation?
choices: The FortiGuard database automatically disables the entire SD-WAN zone
The green arrow on the second server proves all members meet the SLA
The health check should be deleted because it has two servers
Investigate the failing member path and evaluate the active server's quality metrics
feedback: The database does not disable a whole zone just because one target fails.
A responding server does not prove every member meets quality thresholds.
Two-server health checks are supported to help separate server failure from link failure.
Correct: inspect the affected member path and the latency/loss/jitter measured against the active server.

questions.question: During a maintenance window, an engineer compares FortiGate graceful BGP shutdown with BFD. Which distinction is correct?
choices: Both mechanisms advertise gshut and lower the peer's local preference
Graceful shutdown drains route preference; BFD detects liveness and can tear down a session
BFD preserves the route while graceful shutdown immediately withdraws it
Graceful shutdown changes interface carrier state while BFD changes VLAN membership
feedback: BFD does not advertise the gshut community or perform the route-preference drain.
Correct: gshut is a planned routing-policy signal; BFD is a fast failure detector.
The functions are reversed; BFD detects liveness and graceful shutdown changes route preference.
Neither mechanism changes Ethernet carrier state or VLAN membership as its core function.

questions.question: A team sees an IPv6 endpoint register with FortiNAC and an AP authenticate to an access switch. Which statement keeps the two mechanisms separate?
choices: Both events are the same RADIUS transaction and share one client identity
FortiNAC IPv6 support proves every switch can be discovered without IPv4
FortiNAC endpoint IPv6 access and FortiAP wired-uplink 802.1X are separate control paths
FortiAP uplink authentication is completed by the FortiNAC portal over IPv6
feedback: The endpoint and AP are distinct devices and use different access-control flows.
IPv6 endpoint support does not remove the documented IPv4 network-device discovery requirement.
Correct: FortiNAC handles endpoint portal/agent reachability, while FortiAP 802.1X authenticates the AP's wired uplink.
The AP's uplink EAP transaction is between the AP, switch authenticator and RADIUS server, not the NAC portal.
